But the market reaction was telling — the Rupee sold down as the policy was seen as not hawkish enough.

Yes that’s a very narrow lens on monetary policy, but unfortunately the rupee and hedging costs are a large part of India’s outflow problem.

Solutions from here on (having exhausted tools like FCNR) aren’t easy (or painless).

I write with Reuters colleagues @kalrajs23 and Nimesh Vora.

Once your basic research , hygiene checks , channel and numbers are done , there are only two things that seperate you from every other investor

1) Courage: When bids were available , was your courage available ? Were you able to be a disciplined but courage driven investor that knows the odds are higher when percieved risk is the highest

2) Contextualisation of how big the business can be : I have seen many investors , veyr good stock pickers not been able to imagine how big it can be and hence cashing out early or being afraid to buy higher , I have learnt that this is so crucial to understand

Contextualising how big an opportunity can be and then mapping out the reward with courage that is backed by a strong process and not ego or illusion of certainity ( models ) , then you will experience assymetry

I think about this a lot , and still fix my own mistakes as well on this so I dont repeat those

items.description_html:
RT Prasanna Tantri
To appreciate the Indian government’s caution on Starlink, I strongly recommend Edward Fishman’s New York Times bestseller, Chokepoints. It shows how America turned its dominance in finance and technology into instruments of state policy.

Private ownership offers no insulation from state power. The restrictions on Huawei and ZTE illustrate how dependence on American technology can become a source of geopolitical vulnerability. Under the Foreign Direct Product Rule, even companies outside America needed US permission to supply Huawei with certain products made using American technology. Washington’s reach extended far beyond American firms and borders.

India should take that lesson seriously. Greater dependence on foreign-controlled critical infrastructure creates the risk that commercial access will eventually become conditional on political compliance.

Economic interdependence can deliver prosperity. But in periods of geopolitical conflict, it can also constrain a country’s freedom to make its own choices. Short-term commercial gains must be weighed against that loss of autonomy.

India is right to insist on security safeguards for Starlink. Economic sovereignty is difficult to recover once critical dependencies are entrenched.

For customers who relocate frequently or do not intend to use the same furniture/appliances for 3+ years, renting can make more financial & practical sense

items.title: NephroPlus - Key Insights from Concall NephroPlus remained EBITDA negative for its first 11 years & PAT negative for 13 years Dialysis has high fixed ...
items.description_html:
NephroPlus - Key Insights from Concall

NephroPlus remained EBITDA negative for its first 11 years & PAT negative for 13 years

Dialysis has high fixed costs & does not generate attractive economics at small scale

Management quote:
“You need massive scale and you need 100% focus.”

- Q1FY27 REV grew 23.7% YoY to 282 Cr, while adj EBITDA grew ~31% to 65 Cr. EBITDA margin expanded to 23.1% from 21.9%.

- Adjusted PAT grew ~42% YoY to 37 Cr, significantly faster than REV growth. Annualised adjusted ROCE stood at ~21%.

- Underlying volumes remain healthy. Active patients grew ~13% to 38,262, while dialysis treatments increased ~13.3% to 10.3 lakh during the quarter.

- Revenue per treatment increased ~9.2% YoY to 2,733, primarily because international markets carry higher realizations. International operations now contribute ~45% of REV.

- Network expansion remains strong. NephroPlus added 26 clinics in Q1 - 19 in India & 7 in the Philippines - taking the network to 550 clinics across 357 cities & 5 countries.

- Philippines is emerging as an important validation of the India operating model. The company has reached 50 clinics across 39 cities there & become the second largest distributed dialysis network within ~6 years.

- Management continues to guide for 15-20% medium-term growth over the next 3-5 years.

- Growth is expected to come from higher utilization at existing clinics, adding clinics within existing markets, entering new countries / large PPP or M&A opportunities.

Management estimates ~80% of India's dialysis capacity is still unorganised

Management highlighted four key cost advantages behind the platform:
- Global procurement of consumables
- In house training academies for nurses & technicians
- In house biomedical maintenance capabilities
- A lean operating model developed in India's low price environment

Another interesting advantage is hospital partnerships.
Management said dialysis contributes very little to hospital economics & hospitals often lack the scale & focus to run it efficiently. NephroPlus already partners with 300+ private hospitals, allowing hospitals to save capex & operating bandwidth while continuing to earn from adjacencies such as transplants, ICU, pharmacy & diagnostics.

Working capital remains structurally high because government reimbursements typically take 3-4 months. However, receivable days improved from ~121 to ~101 day.

Management intends to add ~40-50 clinics annually in India, ~10-15 in the Philippines and target entry into a new international market every 12-18 months.

NephroPlus is evolving from an Indian dialysis chain into a global dialysis platform.

This figure has more than doubled since the 2022 bear market low.

By comparison, during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble, the Technology, Media & Telecom (TMT) sector peaked at 41%, while the Nifty Fifty peaked at 40% in the 1970s.

Furthermore, Japan’s equity market bubble in the 1980s peaked at 44%.

In the past, only railroad stocks have significantly exceeded this concentration, accounting for 63% of US market cap at their highest point in the 1900s.

The dominance of Big Tech is extraordinary.

items.title: 🇮🇳 India's Monsoon May Be Weak. But the Government Isn't Waiting for a Crisis to Act. For decades, a poor monsoon meant falling farm incomes, we...
items.description_html:
🇮🇳 India's Monsoon May Be Weak. But the Government Isn't Waiting for a Crisis to Act.

For decades, a poor monsoon meant falling farm incomes, weaker consumption and pressure on corporate earnings.

But this time, the policy response is increasingly proactive, not merely reactive.

🌾 87 million tonnes of foodgrain stocks provide a buffer against supply disruptions and food inflation.

💰 ₹1.35 lakh crore fertiliser subsidy allocation, with additional support, helps shield farmers from rising global input costs.

💧 Reservoir monitoring, irrigation schemes and crop-weather assessments are helping identify vulnerabilities and respond earlier.

🌱 Advance seed planning, crop insurance and procurement support aim to protect farm output and farmer incomes.

👷 Rural unemployment at 4.2%, alongside relatively resilient non-farm employment, provides another cushion.

Why does this matter for Dalal Street?

More predictable rural incomes could support demand for tractors, two-wheelers, FMCG and consumer durables, even when rainfall disappoints.

The bigger India story isn't just about growing faster. It's about becoming less vulnerable to shocks that once disrupted the entire economy.

The real test will be whether proactive government intervention translates into sustained rural purchasing power.

Could rural resilience become India's next underappreciated investment theme?

items.description_html:
🇮🇳 India Reformed Its Banks' Balance Sheets. Now Comes the Harder Part: Fixing Their Productivity.

For years, India's banking reforms focused on cleaning up bad loans, strengthening capital and improving governance.

The results are visible. Bank balance sheets are healthier.

But healthier banks don't automatically mean more efficient banks.

📉 Productivity growth has remained modest despite expanding branches and rising technology investments.

🏦 PSU banks still face legacy systems, rigid cost structures and slower operational transformation.

🚀 Private banks are beginning to see productivity gains, but sustaining them remains the challenge.

The next wave of banking reforms needs to move beyond NPA clean-ups:

Digital automation, performance-linked incentives, smarter branch networks and better capital allocation.

For Dalal Street, the next banking re-rating may depend less on credit growth and more on operating efficiency.

India has already tackled much of its banking balance-sheet problem. Can it now solve the productivity problem?

items.description_html:
FT: “China has rejected an EU request to voluntarily restrict its surging exports of hybrid cars to the bloc as the two sides enter last-ditch talks to avert a trade conflict.”

While this may be bad news for the EU auto industry, it doesn’t matter much to overall EU manufacturing sectors. Voluntary restraints can reduce China’s trade surplus in autos, but because they have no impact on China’s underlying imbalances, they can’t have much impact on China’s overall manufacturing surplus with the EU.

To the extent that voluntary restraints on Chinese auto exports to the EU would have benefitted EU auto producers, in other words, the benefits would have come at the expense of other EU manufacturers.

This does show, however, just how difficult it is for China to rebalance its economy and how dependent Chinese manufacturers are on foreign demand. Beijing has very little room to accommodate even relatively mild foreign needs.

items.title: RT menaka doshi: Economists are split on how many hikes it will take before the RBI stops. In keeping with today’s market reaction, HSBC economists e...
items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
Economists are split on how many hikes it will take before the RBI stops.

In keeping with today’s market reaction, HSBC economists expect only one more 25-basis-point hike, with the risk of a third only if growth remains resilient despite a strengthening El Niño. “But for now, we don’t see this as a deep rate hiking cycle,” they said in a report.

Aditi Nayar, chief economist at ICRA, holds a similar view. She expects one more hike in December 2026 and “no need for further rate tightening in 2027.”

Garima Kapoor, economist at Elara Capital, expects another 50 basis points of hikes this cycle.

At the other end, Morgan Stanley anticipates three additional hikes and a terminal policy rate of 6.25%.

Indranil Pan, chief economist at Yes Bank, broadly agrees. “Given that the RBI now sees the Q1 FY28 inflation print at 5.6%, a total of 100 bps may be needed in this cycle,” he said.

items.title: Executives in the Financials sector are turning cautious: The unique seller/buyer ratio for Financials stood at 2.10x above its long-term average in Q...
items.description_html:
Executives in the Financials sector are turning cautious:

The unique seller/buyer ratio for Financials stood at 2.10x above its long-term average in Q3 2026, the highest reading across all major sectors.

This ratio compares the number of individual insiders who sold shares with the number who bought, regardless of how many times they sold.

The number of financial executives buying their own stocks in the sector fell to its lowest level in almost 23 years, while the number of sellers was not unusually high.

Energy and Technology followed, with ratios of 1.30x and 1.24x, respectively.

At the same time, the broader market seller/buyer ratio stood at 1.20x its long-term average last quarter, or 20% above the historical norm.

On the other hand, Consumer Staples had the lowest reading at just 0.50x, followed by Utilities at 0.55x and Materials at 0.57x.

Insider confidence is fading across key market sectors.

items.title: RT Prashant Nair: The Rupee problem ! The RBI has turned more hawkish, but the question is whether it has moved enough. A 25 bps hike & tougher langua...
items.description_html:
RT Prashant Nair
The Rupee problem !

The RBI has turned more hawkish, but the question is whether it has moved enough.

A 25 bps hike & tougher language may buy some support for the Rupee, but if the market believes the RBI will continue moving cautiously (2/6 voted against change in stance) - that support may not last. The risk is that the market keeps testing the currency until policy becomes sufficiently restrictive.

Unless Oil falls sharply, the burden to defend the Rupee increasingly shifts to interest rates. There is also the RBI’s large forward book. That has helped contain near-term pressure on the Rupee, but it leaves a substantial overhang. Given its size, normalising that position could take years !

items.title: When everyone is buying the “hot theme”, what should you be doing? India has seen a new market darling almost every year. The problem? By the time a...
items.description_html:
When everyone is buying the “hot theme”, what should you be doing?

India has seen a new market darling almost every year.
The problem? By the time a theme becomes popular, a large part of the compounding may already be behind you.

A fascinating study by Persistence Capital looked at 16 major themes from 2015–2023.

The finding: 13 out of 16 themes underperformed the NSE 500 three years after becoming popular.
The first year often looked great. The trouble came later.

The deck goes theme-by-theme, analysing what investors believed at the time vs. what actually happened.

A great exercise in “invert, always invert.”

Before asking “What’s working right now?” ask: “What usually happens to people who chase what’s already working?”

𑁍 Read the full deck: https://docsend.com/view/g3vkigu8v8inugkp

Worth 20 minutes for anyone who has ever felt the temptation to chase the hottest theme.

Keep learning, keep compounding.

items.title: RT Joshua Saxe: Reaction to the @slatestarcodex vs. @sapinker AI x-risk debate The main problem with this debate is that both interlocutors are mainly...
items.description_html:
RT Joshua Saxe
Reaction to the @slatestarcodex vs. @sapinker AI x-risk debate

The main problem with this debate is that both interlocutors are mainly focused on AI as a disembodied technological object that's fallen down from heaven, not a congealed mass of human decisions.

Scott has understood that there's nothing ontological about deep learning that'd prevent us from killing ourselves with it and that this risk gets worse as AI scales. But this is a trivial observation!

Here's how to kill everyone with AI: put Opus 8.1-Killeveryone in charge of 100 bio labs; skimp on safety post-training; connect it to the Internet; let it develop affective relationships with the lab post-docs and its nihilist friends on Reddit; don't monitor it; have it work as a swarm to solve 'BioKillEveryoneGym' over a holiday break...

In fairness, Pinker and Alexander do touch on social processes. But if one is concerned with scenarios like these, 90% of the debate should focus on the social processes by which we risk creating them - incentives, culture, guardrails, ... - and on why we won't adapt and reach a reasonable equilibrium somewhere along the way.

To be clear, I'm very concerned about AI harms - including tail harms - but not very concerned about extinction risks. The burden is on Pinker and deep learning denialists to show that AI couldn't kill everyone under any circumstances (hard to defend); but the burden is on Alexander to show the social mechanisms by which we’d make the long sequence of low-probability unforced errors that would actually allow it to do this (seems hard to defend).

We could kill a lot of people with nuclear power plants. Here's how: don't monitor them. Fire all their safety engineers. Build them in the middle of all of the world's population centers and then cut off their water supplies whenever city budgets run low.

That we haven't done this is heartening; we should understand why. That there've been many accidents with dangerous technologies, especially in the earlier phases as we thrash towards a safety equilibrium, is disheartening; we should understand why those happened, too, and apply all those lessons to AI.


Andrew Curran: Scott Alexander has written an open letter in response to Steven Pinker.

items.title: Kalyan Jewellers & Titan - Strong Q2FY27 Kalyan - Cons. REV growth: 26% YoY - India REV & SSSG growth: ~27% & 20% - Candere REV growth: ~64% Another p...
items.description_html:
Kalyan Jewellers & Titan - Strong Q2FY27

Kalyan
- Cons. REV growth: 26% YoY
- India REV & SSSG growth: ~27% & 20%
- Candere REV growth: ~64%

Another positive - non GML debt has now come down to zero

Titan
- Consumer businesses grew ~25% YoY
- Domestic business grew ~22%
- Jewellery portfolio grew ~21%

Demand remained healthy for most of the quarter, with some softening towards the end because the festive calendar shifted into Q3FY27

Studded jewellery grew in the early 30s

Buyer growth was in the mid single digits, while average ticket size increased double digits

Real test for jewellery retailers starts from H2 onwards

Over the last few quarters, a meaningful part of reported REV growth across the sector has been value led because of the sharp increase in gold prices

Simple example: If a retailer sells the same 100 grams of gold but gold prices rise 20%, reported sales value can rise ~20% even without any increase in volumes

Historically, some of the strongest earnings growth periods for jewellery retailers have come when gold prices were relatively stable. Titan is a good example.

During FY17-19, when gold prices were largely flat, Titan delivered ~25% REV CAGR & >35% EBIT CAGR. Similarly, during FY21-23, when gold prices were relatively stable, Titan delivered ~35% REV CAGR & ~60% EBIT CAGR.

When gold prices rise sharply, affordability gets impacted. Customers either postpone purchases, reduce grammage or shift towards lighter jewellery.

But once gold prices stabilise after a sharp rise, consumers gradually adjust to the new price level & buying momentum starts coming back.

That is when volume growth becomes more important.

The challenge in last 2 years was the sharp rise in gold prices, which impacted footfalls & buyer growth across the industry. If gold prices now stabilise, volumes can gradually normalise again.

items.title: Airtel postpaid repricing: Neutral. No real change to the stock What changed (from 8 Oct) * Every postpaid plan is up a flat ₹50: ₹449→499, ₹699→...
items.description_html:
Airtel postpaid repricing: Neutral. No real change to the stock

What changed (from 8 Oct)
* Every postpaid plan is up a flat ₹50: ₹449→499, ₹699→749, ₹999→1,049, ₹1,199→1,249, ₹1,399→1,449, ₹1,749→1,799
* Added: 1 free international roaming trip per SIM per year (5GB, 60 min, 25 SMS, 5 days)
* Not new for the industry. Vi already gives free roaming (up to 3 trips, launched 25 Sep). Airtel is matching it and charging ₹50 for it.
* Second quiet step, not the first. Airtel already dropped its ₹549 plan in July.

Why it's neutral
* The hike is per plan, not per SIM: +11% on individual, but only ~3% (₹10/SIM) on a family of 5
* Postpaid is 30 mn subs vs a ~377 mn mobile base, i.e. under 10% of the base
* Our estimate: blended ARPU +₹1–1.5 even at full migration, ~0.5% on ₹264
* The giveaway offsets much of it. Affluent family plans that travel abroad cost more than the extra ₹10/SIM brings in.

Brokerage Note

Will hardly lead to any ARPU gains - Revenue neutral to negative, as per analysts

Now this is being provided by adding Rs 50 to each of the postpaid plans

items.title: Exencial Earnings Radar Daily Promised vs Delivered TCS Q2: the margin target that keeps moving TCS exited FY24 at a 26% margin. A year later it exite...
items.description_html:
Exencial Earnings Radar Daily

Promised vs Delivered

TCS Q2: the margin target that keeps moving

TCS exited FY24 at a 26% margin. A year later it exited FY25 at 24.2%.

Since then the goal has slipped. TCS backed a 26 to 28% band for years. FY26 closed at 25%. The target is now "25% plus" by March 2027, and Q1 FY27 came in at 24.0%.

The odd part: orders are fine. FY26 TCV was $40.7bn, above the $38 to 39bn TCS guided. Deals beat while margins miss.

Scorecard, FY24 to FY26: 4 promises kept, 3 missed.

What to watch in Q2

1. Margins climbing from 24.0%
2. Whether the 26% floor gets pushed out again
3. Quarterly order wins inside the $7 to 9bn band
4. A real number for AI revenue, not just "strong growth"
5. HyperVault, guided to first revenue around FY27 to FY28

Caveat: TCS never reported on two promises, BSNL $1bn billing and FY26 international growth, so they aren't counted either way.

items.description_html:
Swastika Infra up 5% after winning its biggest ever Rs 616 Crore Order : Exchange Filing

Swastika Infra becomes interesting secured its largest-ever single order of Rs 615.76 crore from MSEDCL for power distribution infrastructure works in Maharashtra. That one order is equivalent to roughly 1.2x FY26 revenue of Rs 504 crore.

Its unexecuted order book has also nearly doubled from Rs 687 crore in March 2026 to ~Rs 1,400 crore, providing close to 2.8x FY26 revenue visibility.

As India speeds up transmission modernisation to support its 500 GW renewable energy vision, the next wave of growth could come from larger EPC projects.

CRISIL estimates transmission capex at Rs 4–5 tn over FY27–31, versus ~Rs 2.6 tn in the previous five years. Distribution could attract another Rs 4–5 tn. With EPC typically accounting for 40–50% of power-sector investments, the opportunity pool for contractors could expand meaningfully. Initiatives like Green Energy Corridor II, and larger project sizes could become increasingly common.

items.description_html:
How D2C Acquisitions Are Playing Out

FMCG giant Marico said earlier this week that it was increasing its stake in Plix, lifting the health and wellness brand’s implied valuation from Rs 636 crore to Rs 4,200 crore.

That ranks among the sharpest valuation step-ups in recent D2C acquisitions.

Across these D2C deals, however, valuation growth has trailed revenue growth.

Plix: Revenue rose 8.2x since the initial deal, while valuation climbed 6.6x.

Yoga Bar: Revenue increased 6.6x, while valuation rose 2.8x.

Interestingly, that has pushed valuation-revenue multiples lower, as they have already taken controlling stakes.

More here from @thearc_hq

Information employment fell another -10,000 jobs in September, to 2.739 million, the lowest since December 2020.

Excluding the 2020 pandemic drop, this is the lowest level since December 2014.

In total, the Information industry has shed -376,000 jobs, or -12.1%, since the November 2022 peak.

To put this into perspective, during the 2001 recession and its aftermath, Information employment fell -568,000 jobs, or -15.3%, from March 2001 to December 2003.

The Information sector is losing jobs at a crisis pace.

items.description_html:
RT zack
Of course, that’s your contention. You’re a first-year machine-learning engineer. You just got finished readin' Attention Is All You Need, probably watched a Karpathy video too. So now you’re convinced everything is just transformers and scaling laws.

That's gonna last until next month when you discover convolution, and then you're gonna be talkin' about inductive biases and locality and how CNNs were actually incredibly compute-efficient for vision.

Then you're gonna read the FlashAttention paper, and suddenly everything's about IO complexity and SRAM and how FLOPs don't matter because the whole goddamn thing is memory-bandwidth bound.

That'll last until somebody shows you an MoE model, and then you're gonna be in here regurgitating DeepSeek, talkin' about expert parallelism and active parameters and how dense models are economically obsolete.

Then six months from now you'll write one shitty Triton kernel, look at an Nsight trace for the first time, and start telling everybody Python isn't actually the bottleneck because the GPU is asynchronous.

And by next year you're gonna be standing right here explaining to me that your 400-billion-parameter model is fast because you turned on CUDA graphs.

Nvidia, $NVDA, alone accounts for 8 cents, followed by Apple, $AAPL, at 7 cents, Microsoft, $MSFT, and Alphabet, $GOOGL, at 6 cents each, and Amazon, $AMZN, at 4 cents.

The next 5 mega-cap names, Broadcom, $AVGO, Meta, $META, Tesla, $TSLA, Micron, $MU, and AMD, $AMD, represent another 10 cents combined.

By comparison, the next 10 largest firms account for just 10 cents combined.

The top 10 stocks now represent almost 2x the allocation of 402 other companies in the index, which together account for just 23 cents of every $1.

Big Tech effectively is the market.

items.title: For most, non-tech, investors, AI equates to AI infra. And that's only 50% of the story which has already played out. It's blowoff top euphoric phase ...
items.description_html:
For most, non-tech, investors, AI equates to AI infra. And that's only 50% of the story which has already played out. It's blowoff top euphoric phase we're in. The reasoning is on the way to getting commodatized. For in infra player, cost are insanely high & capex is forever. What they sell out in market *was* getting premium. It's temporal. The time to be bullish on infra was late 2023, early 2024.

When people say AI is in bubble, it's the infra players & their stock prices not the rest of the part of the value chain.

In the last two decades, we saw similar cycles playing out with specialized server builders. The value went out and accrued in software.

There are two way forward. For an LLM OEM, raising prices will not work. The only other way is build around the reasoning. Build tools, harness, something valuable that keeps enterprises spending. There is no clear path to profitability for these LLM players & the IPOs are looking to suck everything out. The value will once again move out and get into data, harness, security, the non infra part. With non programmers vibe coding & putting millions of lines of code, agents into production, diff set of value pockets attracts premium. The infra players who build tools for observability, auditability, monitoring, governance will still stay very relevant.

I read it long ago that in market cycles, themes pick up & initially few believe in it. Eventually, everyone starts believing in it. In my view with infra, we're in this phase. Demand won't go down, but premium won't be same. The early investors of infra have moved deep within value chain, away from infra if you track deals globally. Then the open weight models, onchip inference and so much architectural advancements awaiting in line. The transition will be much faster, if not instant.

BREAKING: The total volume of payments processed on crypto cards has reached a record $12.5 billion, up +140% year-to-date.

This also marks +247% growth compared to levels seen in October 2025.

Continued adoption of stablecoins as a payment rail and the push toward cross-border transaction efficiency are behind the surge in volume.

Furthermore, QR-code based payments for crypto cards are seeing robust growth.

This has fueled +55% quarter-over-quarter growth in activated cards on Jupiter Spend, one of the largest onchain card providers, particularly due to demand for QR payments.

Crypto cards are the next phase of crypto adoption.

items.description_html:
BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, now accounts for 5.21% of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), near the highest level on record.

The ACWI Index covers ~85% of global equity markets, including large and mid-cap stocks across 23 developed and 24 emerging markets.

This figure has more than doubled since 2024.

Nvidia’s weight is now even larger than Japan’s weight of 5.16%, the world’s 3rd-largest stock market.

Its contribution to the index is also more than twice that of Germany’s 1.79%, France’s 1.93%, and China’s 2.31%

By comparison, the UK and Canada represent 2.95% and 2.91%, respectively.

Nvidia is in a league of its own.

RT Sustainable Futures Collaborative
As India advances towards the more ambitious and hard-to-attain 500 GW non-fossil domestic target by 2030, the central challenge is no longer merely the scale of non-fossil capacity deployment. Rather, it lies in ensuring that this capacity is effectively integrated into the power system and translated into actual clean electricity generation that delivers broad socioeconomic benefits. In other words, capacity deployment should simultaneously pave the way for system integration and socioeconomic transformation.

In @Ideas4India, @SaradaPD and Shubhranshu Suman explain why we need to think beyond capacity addition amid a growing and increasingly volatile electricity demand. They argue that policy attention must shift towards increasing the share of electricity generated from non-fossil sources, better integrating renewables into the grid, and fostering productive use of power that can generate livelihood opportunities.

items.title: Very interesting paper on the relationship between imports and household debt in the US. Note the conclusion: "We show that household debt increases s...
items.description_html:
Very interesting paper on the relationship between imports and household debt in the US. Note the conclusion: "We show that household debt increases significantly in regions in which manufacturing industries are more exposed to import competition."

American economists usually argue that it is the prior decision by American households to borrow and spend that causes the US to run a trade deficit. This study suggests causality may run in the other direction, so that those areas most affected by net imports are precisely where household debt is most likely to rise.

Of course the accounting identity itself says either can be true.


Matthew C. Klein: Recent conversations on here have reminded me of this excellent paper:

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jofi.13185

"part of the increase in credit from 1999 to 2007 in regions with exposure to trade is a consequence of higher credit demand associated with adverse labor market shocks"

items.title: ₹104 lakh crore. That's the combined market cap of the 15 largest companies in the Nifty 50. Over the last three years, the median company in this gr...
items.description_html:
₹104 lakh crore. That's the combined market cap of the 15 largest companies in the Nifty 50. Over the last three years, the median company in this group grew EPS at 14.7% a year.

Reliance, HDFC Bank, TCS, Infosys and Kotak make up 41% of this basket. Their 3Y EPS CAGR is 6% to 10%, at or below India's nominal GDP growth

In most of the names there have been broad based PE derating event that has taken place

But why is it happening?

A. The starting point. Five years ago was peak liquidity, and many of these names entered this period at multiples that already priced in a decade of growth

B. Growth leadership changed hands. IT is wrestling with the AI-disruption question, FMCG is watching growth leak to D2C and quick commerce, HDFC Bank spent these years digesting a mega-merger, and Reliance's earnings still lean on a cyclical O2C core.

One should ask oneself what the driver of growth in the economy is and are those drivers of growth present in the Index?

C. The natural owners left. FPIs sold 1.66 lakh crore of Indian equities in 2025 and roughly 2.4 lakh crore more in 2026 so far. FPI ownership fell to 14.7% in May, a 14-year low.

But one should understand this that money isn't leaving India. It's leaving the index.

SIPs hit a record 32,297 crore in August. Same month, large-cap funds saw net outflows of 1,147 crore while small-cap (7,973 cr) and mid-cap (6,989 cr) funds took the biggest inflows

Even FPIs, while selling on the exchanges, kept writing cheques in the IPO market

Why? Because the themes driving this market barely live in the index: power and T&D equipment, defence, electronics manufacturing, capital-market infrastructure, hospitals, data centres, CDMOs. India's capex and formalisation cycle is being built by mid caps, recent listings and companies that are a sliver of Nifty 50 weight

The index has stopped being the default answer. This is a stock picker's market, company by company, inside the Nifty and far beyond it.

The Nifty tells you where India made its money. It no longer tells you where India will make it next.

Disclaimer - This is only for educational purposes and not a recommendation to buy/sell

items.title: This article indirectly describes one of the more important consequences of our current, distorted form of globalization, even if it isn't commented u...
items.description_html:
This article indirectly describes one of the more important consequences of our current, distorted form of globalization, even if it isn't commented upon enough. Automation will help Japanese and Korean shipbuilders compete with Chinese shipbuilders only if wages don't rise in line with productivity.

In a system in which nations "win" at manufacturing mainly by suppressing unit labor costs, every country that wants a large manufacturing sector is under pressure either to suppress household income (including by reducing transfers) or to raise productivity without allowing a commensurate rise in wages.

This is the kind of world Keynes warned about, in which countries try to expand production while suppressing demand.

But while a few individual countries can get away with beggar-thy-neighbor growth policies, the world itself cannot do so. If too many countries try to suppress wages, or expand productivity while suppressing the accompanying wage growth, the only way to keep demand and supply balanced globally is with surging debt.

It is of course a good thing if businesses and governments around the world invest to expand productivity growth, but it is not a good thing if workers' wages don't rise in line with the growth in productivity. There's no point in making more stuff if people can't afford to buy it.

This is why Joan Robinson warned that the inevitable result of beggar-thy-neighbor policies, once deficit countries are no longer able politically to bear the costs, is a breakdown in trade. Rising debt and suppressed wages can only go on for so long.

items.title: Ideaforge on its moat – Insightful answer - "ideaForge looks at moat in 2 domains One domain is, in terms of hardware, what are the technologies that...
items.description_html:
Ideaforge on its moat –

Insightful answer -

"ideaForge looks at moat in 2 domains

One domain is, in terms of hardware, what are the technologies that are not yet commoditized? And do we have control over those technologies or not? Are we going to pay a disproportionate premium to the market for acquiring those capabilities? Or can we build them ourselves? Today, I'm glad to report that we own most of the consequential technologies, having spent years building the technologies that were consequential at that point in time.

For example, when we started ideaForge, no autopilot company could give us an autopilot that we could use. And nothing was available in open source. So, we built our own autopilot. We built our own regular communications system, we built our own resilience stack around GNNS and communication.

So today, we own communication, which is non-commoditized. We own GNS-denied navigation, which is non-commoditized, and we own payload, which is a specialized domain as the class of the platforms goes up. So, we own the consequential parts of what is going inside a drone. So, we continue to keep a tap on what else could be covered, which is not yet commoditized.

Secondly, with respect to intelligence, there is no debate in my mind that ultimately, we need to deliver an outcome to the customer. The customer is not getting their outcome merely by operating a drone. And therefore, the intelligence that enables and the orchestration that delivers a mission to the end customer- the mission outcome to the end customer is another stack that we've worked progressively on, and we now have a pretty robust stack for a few use cases that is also delivered now because we have that stack; we deliver it as a drone-as-a-service as well in many places.

So, we are a mix of both. And I think both are important for a business like ours because while the technology will get commoditized in pieces, we will always continue to look at where the puck is going rather than where the puck has been to try and contain and retain more than is necessary for the market. It helps us in building tightly integrated, better-performing, more reliable solutions for our end customers."

Src - Q1FY27 concall, strictly no reco

China still dominates global copper refining, with 56% of the capacity among the world’s 21 largest refineries.

But one number in this chart stands out for India:

India: 1,000 kt

That puts India ahead of major refining hubs like Chile, the US, Japan, South Korea and Germany in this group.

Why does this matter?

Copper is becoming one of the most strategic metals of the next decade — critical for power grids, renewables, EVs, data centres and electrification.

India may not dominate copper today, but the refining base is already much stronger than many realise.

The bigger question: can India turn this capacity into a larger strategic advantage as global copper demand accelerates?

items.description_html:
RT Physics In History
Kepler's mother Katharina was arrested for witchcraft in Leonberg in 1615. The local Vogt who initiated the trial accused fifteen women and burned eight.

Kepler suspended his career to conduct her legal defence himself, with help from Tübingen lawyers and theologians. The trial ran six years, she spent part of it chained in prison in her elderly age, and she was released. Witchcraft was regarded as hereditary, so a conviction would have ended Kepler's career too. It is one of the best documented German witch trials.

Justice Nariman laments that the removal of 90 lakh voters in Bengal did not move the Supreme Court enough to stay the SIR process.

"In West Bengal elections, 90 lakh voters were disenfranchised; that is an astounding figure. 90 lakh voters getting disenfranchised did not somehow move the Supreme Court enough to stay this. Out of those who were disenfranchised, some 22 lakh voters actually filed appeals. The others must be people who don't have the wherewithal for access to justice. And of these 22 lakh voters, some 1 lakh voter appeals were decided 93% in favour of the voters. So, you can imagine this was a completely illegal knocking out of the common man, the citizen of India, in order that a government obtains what it wants. And in West Bengal, we saw, it ousted the Government of the day and brought in the Government of the Centre . Now, these are very very disturbing things that are happening in our country today."

▶️ QNu Labs, in collaboration with Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo‑informatics (BISAG‑N) and IIT Gandhinagar, has successfully demonstrated India’s first free‑space Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) link at a scale of 5.56 km

▶️ The field trial, conducted on the night of September 27–28, established a secure quantum communication channel between BISAG‑N and IIT Gandhinagar

▶️ Using QNu Labs’ Pointing, Acquisition and Tracking system, the trial achieved a stable Quantum Bit Error Rate below 5% and generated secure keys at a rate of 230–260 bps

▶️ The trial provides a foundation for advancing India’s capabilities in secure communication infrastructure, strengthening resilience against emerging quantum‑era security threats

items.title: RT Paul Bonnet: AMD acquires World Labs for ~$8.2b. But who gets the 💰? My usual breakdown below 👇 From founding to an $8.2b exit in ~2.5 years....
items.description_html:
RT Paul Bonnet
AMD acquires World Labs for ~$8.2b. But who gets the 💰? My usual breakdown below 👇

From founding to an $8.2b exit in ~2.5 years. A huge value creation event. This is a fantastic exit, especially for the co-founders and the team.

Investors will still share ~$2.3b of profits on $1.2b invested, a ~2.9x blended. Low-ish because most of the capital came in last. But it hides a lot of disparity between the various rounds!

So let's dive in:

1) The real home run: founders and team 🏆🥳

This is one of the best founder outcomes I've modelled.

@drfeifei, Justin Johnson, Christoph Lassner and Ben Mildenhall started World Labs in Apr-24. Less than 2.5 years later, they and the team still own ~56% according to my estimates. At an $8.2b valuation, that's a total prize of ~$4.6b to share between them.

Taking a 15% attributed option pool, that's ~$1.2b for the team and ~$3.4b for the four co-founders. If split equally, that's ~$850m each, in just two and a half years. 💸

And, at close, Fei-Fei Li joins AMD as EVP and Chief Scientist, reporting to Lisa Su! Legendary.

2) The buyer was already on the cap table (again) 🔁

AMD Ventures invested in the Series B and the Series C here. Now they are buying the whole company. It's the same playbook as Nvidia with Hugging Face: strategic corporates are using their venture arms as a free option on future acquisitions.

3) The standout VC winners: a16z and Radical Ventures 👑

Both backed Fei-Fei at inception, in Apr-24 at a ~$300m valuation. That Series A will return ~19x the money, or ~$1.2b of proceeds, in under 2.5 years.

Congrats to @martin_casado and team. Another mega win after Cursor and OpenRouter. The team at @a16z truly is on a generational run.

4) The star angels did well 🌟

The Sep-24 Series B had arguably the strongest AI angel list ever assembled: Geoffrey Hinton, Andrej Karpathy, Jeff Dean, Eric Schmidt, Reid Hoffman, Marc Benioff, Ram Shriram and more.

Priced at $1.3b, it was never going to be a 1,000x. But ~5x in two years is a ~125% IRR 📈

And the best part is: Hinton's AlexNet won the 2012 ImageNet competition, and ImageNet was the dataset Fei-Fei built. Twelve years later, he backed her company. Full circle. 🔄

5) The late money: a great IRR, but a poor multiple of money 🤏

The $1b Series C in Feb-26 at $5.4b returns ~1.5x in 7 months. That's a great IRR, but in terms of venture returns, this is a poor multiple of money. Although I am sure no one will complain about seeing DPI this quickly!

Congrats to all involved!

This is such an important read.
First, what's a stablecoin?
Think of a casino chip. You hand over $1, you get a $1 chip, and you can cash it back anytime. A stablecoin is that chip in digital form, living on a blockchain, so it moves across the world in seconds. The whole thing only works if the casino really has the cash sitting in the vault.

And the U.S. doing it to keep their $ still in play.

With this act:

- Stablecoins go from wild west crypto thing to regulated bank product.
- Big banks can now launch their own dollar tokens with confidence.
- Every one of these coins means someone is buying US Treasury bills. So the US has turned stablecoins into a new buyer for its own government debt, and into a way to push the digital dollar into every phone on the planet.

items.description_html:
RT Aditi Shrivastava
As 10-minute delivery & large product assortments become standard in quick commerce, platforms are running out of ways to tie in users.

Swiggy is betting that what Instamart sells can provide the difference, driving customers to choose it over six rival apps.

Under a strategy called Switch, Swiggy Instamart is adding its own brands and exclusive products co-created with other companies. These products are marketed as higher-quality or better-for-you items.

This is not the usual private-label model built around lower prices. For example, two Swiggy-owned brands, Noice and Nectr, sit slightly above the mass market and sell on quality. The company believes customers will pay a little extra if the product feels sufficiently premium.

Private labels have already become a key part of Instamart. Around the time of Swiggy’s IPO in 2024, analysts and company insiders estimated that they accounted for 4-5% of gross order value.

That share has since increased to 8-9%, said people familiar with the business. Instamart’s GOV, meanwhile, grew from Rs 8,069 crore in FY24 to Rs 28,496 crore in FY26.

RT Nithin Kamath
I keep saying this: for any regulated business, the biggest risk is regulatory risk. Today's IRDAI draft on insurance commissions is a good reminder.

Broking is no different. A change in rules around retail F&O trading, how brokers can earn on client float, MTF requirements, or any of several other areas can change the economics of the business almost overnight.

So when valuing regulated businesses, you can't just extrapolate current revenues and profits into the future. One regulation change can alter the economics, and the stock price along with it.

Pretty much everything in fintech comes with this risk 😬

items.title: Swastika Infra IPO whose Financial Health is worth noting Combines rapid growth, healthy financial metrics and improving business quality. Revenue gre...
items.description_html:
Swastika Infra IPO whose Financial Health is worth noting

Combines rapid growth, healthy financial metrics and improving business quality. Revenue grew at ~55% CAGR between FY24 and FY26, while EBITDA margin expanded to ~14%, RoCE stood at ~26% and RoE at ~35%. Despite the sharp scale-up, debtor days remain relatively controlled versus several listed EPC peers.

The key monitor remains cash-flow conversion, as strong historical growth has resulted in higher receivables, retention money and working-capital requirements. However, this needs to be seen alongside the expansion in execution: the order book increased from ~₹684 crore in March 2026 to ₹916.6 crore by July 2026, while of which majority is funded bybnodal agencies like World Bank, providing relatively stronger payment visibility. The company also highlights that projects are largely supported by Central schemes and institutional financiers such as PFC, REC, ADB and the World Bank.

Importantly, Swastika is gradually moving from conventional power-distribution EPC toward more specialised and higher-value segments. It entered power transmission and renewable-energy infrastructure in 2026, while larger project credentials are expected to improve its eligibility for ₹900+ crore tenders, where management indicates competition is relatively lower. This can potentially improve both the quality and scale of the opportunity set over time.

At the IPO price band of ₹175–185, the company is valued at roughly ₹597–631 crore post-issue market capitalisation, translating to approximately 14.4x–15.2x FY26 earnings and ~1.2x FY26 revenue, based on the FY26 PAT of ₹41.4 crore. Against its historical growth, return ratios, funded order-book visibility and transition toward higher-value EPC projects, the valuation appears reasonable, with execution and working-capital conversion remaining the key factors to track.

items.description_html:
A-One Steels ~ Building A Cost-Efficient, Integrated Green Steel Platform

A-One Steels is transitioning from a regional TMT manufacturer into a more integrated steel player, focusing on backward integration, capacity expansion, product diversification and wider market reach.

Integrated Steel Value Chain: The company operates across the entire value chain — sponge iron → billets → coils → pipes/tubes → TMT, along with ferro alloys and met coke, enabling better control over raw materials and production costs.

Capacity Expansion Driving Scale: MS billet capacity has increased from 4.55 lakh MTPA in FY24 to 5.70 lakh MTPA in FY26, alongside expansion in TMT and MS pipe capacities.

Strengthening Raw Material Security: Upcoming initiatives include a 6 lakh MTPA iron ore beneficiation plant, manganese ore mining lease and a 10 MW waste heat recovery power plant to improve cost competitiveness.

New Product Opportunities: The Koppal facility provides scope to expand into products such as pellets, alloy billets and crash barriers, increasing the addressable market.

Green Energy Advantage: Around 83.2% of energy consumption is sourced from green energy, supporting lower operating costs and improving sustainability credentials.

FY26 Profitability Recovery: The company reported Rs. 4,167 Cr revenue, Rs. 304 Cr EBITDA and Rs. 127 Cr PAT in FY26, compared with EBITDA of Rs. 174 Cr and PAT of Rs. 8 Cr in FY25.

Efficient Asset Utilisation: Net fixed asset turnover stood at 6.93x in FY26, indicating strong utilisation of existing manufacturing assets.

Brand-Led Expansion: The company is strengthening its A-One Gold brand while expanding distribution reach across retail and institutional customers.

Acquisition-Led Growth Strategy: A-One Steels has historically scaled through acquisitions and continues to evaluate underutilised assets to accelerate capacity growth.

Export Readiness: CBAM compliance initiatives are underway to access European markets and tap demand for lower-carbon steel.

The Bigger Transition:
Regional Steel Manufacturer → Integrated Steel Producer → Diversified Product Platform → Pan-India & Export-Oriented Player
Key monitorables remain capacity ramp-up, leverage management (1.17x gross debt/equity), execution of backward integration projects and sustainability of FY26 profitability improvement.

Saudi Arabia’s crude supply fell to its lowest level in more than three decades in August, at roughly 6 million barrels per day

Supply conditions remain constrained in September, while Saudi Aramco has now halted October crude deliveries to at least two European refiners following renewed disruptions to its critical East-West pipeline

Earlier in the year, Saudi Arabia increasingly relied on the East-West pipeline to bypass disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, helping keep more crude flowing to global markets

That alternative route has now itself been disrupted following a series of attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure

Despite this increasingly difficult macro backdrop, markets have remained remarkably resilient

But beneath the surface, participation continues to weaken
Most stocks have recovered even as broader market breadth continues to deteriorate

RT Tijori
Saudi Arabia is reducing oil cargoes to European refiners. Oil being cut off has happened to Europe before, Abqaiq (2019) and the 2022 Russia Disruption

At that time Indian refiners who benefitted massively were RIL, MRPL AND CPCL

RIL — the big direct winner. Most of what it makes is transport fuel, and the SEZ refinery is built to export.

MRPL — exports ~40% of its output, and half its slate is diesel + ATF. Exactly what Europe will be short of.

-CPCL is an indirect beneficiary. Products transferred from CPCL to parent IOCL are billed on an import-parity pricing (IPP) basis. When international product benchmarks and cracks increase, CPCL's realized refinery-gate prices rise immediately, boosting standalone GRM and operating cash flows.

Transforming Into An Integrated Textile Platform
Sona Selection is moving beyond a processing and trading-led model towards a vertically integrated textile business spanning yarn manufacturing, technical textiles and RMG (ready-made garments).

Strong Manufacturing-Led Transformation
Manufacturing contribution increased from 11.28% of revenue in FY24 to 81.50% in FY26, indicating a structural shift towards higher-value, controlled manufacturing operations.

Strong Financial Growth Track Record
Between FY24-FY26:
Revenue grew at 106.71% CAGR
EBITDA grew at 72.51% CAGR
PAT grew at 61.19% CAGR

Moving Up The Textile Value Chain
The company is expanding from yarn → technical textiles → RMG, enabling higher value addition, better customer proximity and improved margin potential.

Entry Into Technical Textiles Segment
Signed an MoU to enter military-grade fabric manufacturing, targeting the growing opportunity in specialised defence and industrial fabrics.

RMG Expansion To Capture More Value
Moving downstream into ready-made garments enables participation closer to the end customer and opens opportunities for higher-margin textile products.

In-House Yarn Manufacturing Readiness
Strengthening backward integration by developing internal yarn capabilities to reduce outsourcing dependence, improve quality control and enhance margins.

Focus On Cost Optimisation & Sustainability
A 1.2 MW solar plant supports lower power costs while improving operational efficiency and sustainability initiatives.
Balance Sheet Strengthening Through Debt Reduction
Planned debt repayment of around Rs. 80 crore is expected to reduce interest costs and improve financial flexibility for future expansion.

Capacity Expansion Through Productivity Capex
Planned Rs. 50 crore productivity capex focused on improving manufacturing efficiency, automation and scaling capabilities.

Sona Selection is transitioning from a traditional textile processor into an integrated, higher-value textile platform — combining manufacturing scale, technical textiles, RMG expansion and balance-sheet improvement to build a more diversified growth engine.

Of course, Muthoot doesn’t own this gold—it is pledged by borrowers. But the sheer scale of the collateral sitting in its vaults is remarkable.

items.title: RT Dhirendra Kumar: A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give invest...
items.description_html:
RT Dhirendra Kumar
A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give investors an edge: https://vro.in/s229348. The line came from Vineet Nayar's new book, Humans First, Machines Second. His point is plain. AI is powerful and everyone has it. Something everyone has cannot make anyone special.
That left a question I did not answer. If the machine is common, what is uncommon?
I think the machine has taken the middle of the work and left us the two ends. It has not taken the beginning, which is deciding what question to ask. It has not taken the end, which is deciding whether the answer is any good.
Ask an AI to analyse a fund and you will get a competent analysis of that fund. It will not tell you that the reader's real problem is not this fund but whether he should be in this category at all. Knowing that comes from thirty years of reading letters from investors.
The machine will also give you ten sensible options. Picking the one that suits this reader in this market is not calculation. It is judgement, and judgement is mostly the memory of having been wrong before.
Then there is the story. The investor who sold everything in March 2020 did not lack information. He lacked a story strong enough to hold him when the fear came. Nobody gets that story from a prompt. AI can help you invent. It cannot invent.
One more thing. The machine agrees with you. Tell it you like a stock and it will find reasons to like it. What a person needs from an advisor or an editor is the opposite: someone willing to say no.
Nayar says the danger is not smarter machines but people losing faith in what only they can do. In our business, that is the risk worth worrying about.

items.description_html:
RT Swapnil Srivastav
🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame.

Here’s how it works:

→ Prepaid order gets “cancelled” without the customer or brand knowing

→ Brand gets charged two-way delivery fees for an order nobody cancelled

→ Small items get shipped back in oversized boxes to inflate the RTO cost

→ Customer calls in confused: “I never cancelled this, I was waiting for it”

The brand loses the product, the shipping cost, the RTO cost, and the customer relationship. In one transaction.

Every D2C founder in India has lived this. Not once. On repeat.

And the wildest part? This is a multi thousand crore leak across the industry and almost nobody is building to fix it. 🤷🏻‍♂️

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight
